content: 1. Women who become pregnant during clinical trials involving TDF/FTC or DTG-based regimens are required to discontinue the study drug. However, they are followed up to monitor pregnancy outcomes. As of May 2018, 12 pregnancies have been reported in the ARIA trial, which is recruiting participants in Russia. Approximately 3% of the participants are female, and 80% are receiving first-line treatment. 2. By May 2018, 363 women on dolutegravir (DTG) had become pregnant. Of these, 361 switched to non-DTG regimens (e.g., efavirenz or raltegravir) after pregnancy diagnosis. Among the outcomes: 77 live births 2 stillbirths 8 abortions 275 pregnancies were ongoing 2 women remained on DTG, resulting in 1 live birth and 1 case under investigation. 3. No cases of birth defects have been reported in the investigated pregnancies in Kenya. DTG rollout began in July 2017 but excluded pregnant women. Most prescriptions were for first-line treatment. Pharmacovigilance systems were in place, but they did not specifically monitor for birth defects. 4. As of March 2018, 11,088 individuals were on DTG in Kenya, with 75% being female. It is estimated that approximately 10% of these women may have become pregnant, but data on pregnancy outcomes are not yet available. 5. Various organizations, including ICAP, UNITAID, CHAI, and the Ministry of Health, are collaborating to integrate data systems. The CDC has implemented a pilot birth defect surveillance program in four hospitals in Uganda, modeled after the Botswana program. PEPFAR also supports a birth surveillance program in Kampala, Uganda, with a nested case-control study. 6. Data on birth defects, including neural tube defects (NTDs), were presented at CROI 2018. Surveillance efforts are ongoing, with approximately 80,000 births monitored to date. Data collection forms are being modified in Nigeria to include information on DTG exposure. 7. UNITAID has initiated a pilot DTG program in Nigeria, requiring contraception for women of childbearing age. As a result, the number of pregnancies is expected to be low. Data on pregnancies are not yet available. 8. Malawi and Zambia are preparing to start DTG programs but have not yet initiated them. Both countries are believed to have PEPFAR-funded birth surveillance programs. 9. WHO, CDC, NIH, UNITAID, and other stakeholders are working together to identify additional opportunities to monitor preconception DTG exposures. Approximately 600 preconception DTG exposures are expected to result in births within the next nine months as part of the Tsepamo study. 10. Proposed activities include: Expanding the Tsepamo study to additional sites in Botswana, with suggestions for ultrasound surveillance and case-control studies. Reviewing pregnancy outcomes in Brazil, where 363 pregnancies in women on DTG have been identified, most of which are ongoing. Expanding PEPFAR-sponsored birth surveillance in Uganda to include DTG exposure data. Implementing birth surveillance or evaluating pregnancy outcomes in Kenya, where approximately 11,000 adults have started DTG. Evaluating pregnancies with DTG exposure in Nigeria, where a small pilot program is underway with UNITAID sponsorship. Assessing preconception DTG exposure outcomes in the Pediatric HIV/AIDS Cohort Study in the U.S. 11. The Antiretroviral Pregnancy Registry (APR) continues to collect data, with the next review scheduled for October 2018. Communication with ongoing adult clinical trials is being maintained to monitor pregnancies. 12. Retrospective APR data have identified two cases of NTDs associated with preconception raltegravir exposure, not dolutegravir. These cases involved mothers with HIV and HCV co-infection. One case resulted in a live birth with hydrocephalus and myelomeningocele, while the other involved a spontaneous abortion with encephalocele. 13. Since May 2018, two additional cases of NTDs with preconception DTG exposure in the U.S. have been reported to the FDA/APR. One case involved a 29-year-old Hispanic woman on DTG since 2015, with an ongoing pregnancy diagnosed with anencephaly. Another case involved a 23-year-old woman with a history of seizures, whose infant was diagnosed with meningocele and neural migration disorder. 14. Retrospective case reports are considered less reliable than prospective cases due to potential reporting bias. Prospective cases are reported during pregnancy and followed up for birth outcomes, while retrospective cases are reported after delivery and may overrepresent abnormalities. 15. Appendix 1 provides a detailed review of all studies, their characteristics, and individual data summaries. Appendix 2 summarizes birth defects by study, type of defect, and trimester of exposure, with data from ViiV, WHO VigiaAccess, and FDA databases.
